cards.front: Recall a key point about Composites and Smart Materials
cards.back: Composites: matrix + reinforcement. CFRP: carbon fibres in epoxy - exceptional strength-to-weight, F1 cars, aircraft. GFRP (fibreglass): glass fibres in polyester resin - lighter than metals, corrosion resistant.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composites and Smart Materials
cards.back: Concrete: aggregate + cement + water - excellent compressive strength, reinforced with steel rebar for tensile strength.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composites and Smart Materials
cards.back: Thermochromic materials: change colour at specific temperatures - baby spoons, mood rings, kettles, bath plugs.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composites and Smart Materials
cards.back: Shape-memory alloys (SMA): Nitinol (nickel-titanium) - deformed at room temperature, returns to original shape when heated. Medical stents, orthodontic wires.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Composites and Smart Materials
cards.back: Piezoelectric materials: generate voltage when mechanically stressed - quartz watches, push-button lighters, energy-harvesting floor tiles.

cards.front: What should you know about d&t exam tips?
cards.back: For composite/smart material questions: 1) Define the material type, 2) Explain the mechanism, 3) State properties, 4) Give applications, 5) Evaluate advantages and limitations.
Smart (e.g. Absorbs large volumes of water)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Composites are always better than single materials because they combine the best of both components. Correct: Composites combine components for specific improvements but also inherit limitations: CFRP is incredibly strong along fibres but weak across them (anisotropic); expensive, difficult to repair, virtually impossible to recycle.
